subject: Mathematics
title: Pythagoras Theorem
learningOutcomes: Identify the hypotenuse and legs of a right-angled triangle.
Find the hypotenuse using \(c=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\), given both legs.
Find a missing leg using \(a=\sqrt{c^{2}-b^{2}}\), given the hypotenuse and one leg.
Apply the theorem to real-life problems such as ladders, cables and rectangle diagonals.
Use the converse of the theorem to test whether a triangle is right-angled.
Recognise Pythagorean triples and their scaled multiples.

sections.heading: The theorem
sections.body: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\), where \(c\) is the hypotenuse and \(a, b\) are the legs. It only applies to right-angled triangles.

sections.heading: Identifying the hypotenuse
sections.body: The hypotenuse is the side directly opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest side. The other two sides, which meet at the right angle, are called the legs (or catheti).

sections.heading: Finding a missing side
sections.body: To find the hypotenuse when both legs are known, use \(c=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) (add the squares, then root). To find a missing leg when the hypotenuse and one leg are known, use \(a=\sqrt{c^{2}-b^{2}}\) (subtract the squares, then root).

sections.heading: Real-life applications
sections.body: The theorem models many everyday right-triangle situations: a ladder leaning against a wall (ladder = hypotenuse), the diagonal of a rectangle (diagonal² = length² + breadth²), the height of an isosceles triangle (height bisects the base at a right angle), and the diagonal size of a screen.

sections.heading: The converse of the theorem
sections.body: If a triangle's three sides \(a, b, c\) (with \(c\) the longest) satisfy \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\), the triangle must be right-angled, with the right angle opposite \(c\). If they do not satisfy this, the triangle is not right-angled — no angle measurement is needed.

sections.heading: Pythagorean triples
sections.body: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers \(a, b, c\) with \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\), such as \((3,4,5)\), \((5,12,13)\) and \((8,15,17)\). Multiplying every number in a triple by the same positive number always gives another valid triple.

definitions.definition: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
The two sides of a right-angled triangle that meet at the right angle.
A triangle containing one angle of exactly \(90^\circ\).
Three positive whole numbers a, b, c satisfying \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\), such as (3, 4, 5).
Testing whether a triangle is right-angled from its three side lengths alone.
A line joining two non-adjacent corners of a shape, often the hypotenuse of a right triangle inside it.

examTips: When finding the hypotenuse, ADD the squares of the legs. When finding a leg, SUBTRACT the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square.
Always check which side is opposite the right angle before deciding which side is the hypotenuse.
For the converse, square the longest side separately and compare it to the sum of the squares of the other two — a close-looking number is not the same as an exact match.
